papers.abstract: We study multilevel optimization problems in which the outer objective depends on a finite composition of implicit response maps defined by smooth inner functions. This model covers chains of strongly convex minimization responses, strongly convex--strongly concave saddle responses, or a mixture of the two. We propose a fully first-order method that estimates the outer gradient through recursive response perturbations. The main difficulty with approximate responses is that an adjoint error at one level changes the perturbation vector at the preceding level. To control this propagation, we pair the unperturbed and perturbed updates at each level and track their scaled differences jointly with the forward response errors. The resulting tracking bounds are uniform in the perturbation radius $δ$. For the exact composite objective, we establish an $O(K^{-1}+δ^2)$ bound on the average squared gradient norm after $K$ outer iterations. For fixed problem data and finite depth, a suitable choice of $δ$ yields $ε$-stationarity in $O(ε^{-2})$ outer iterations with inner budgets independent of the target accuracy. For strongly convex minimization chains, we also derive condition-number-dependent first-order oracle complexity bounds.

papers.title: Equivalence of Restricted and Full Division
papers.abstract: We prove over $\mathrm{PA}^{-}$ that the restricted Euclidean division principle $\mathrm{pa17}^{-}$, which asserts division only for co-prime pairs, is equivalent to the full principle $\mathrm{pa17}$. The proof uses a transformation that preserves the quotient in division with remainder to reduce an arbitrary division problem to one for a co-prime pair. This answers Visser's Open Question 8.29 and shows that the restricted principle has the same strength as full Euclidean division over $\mathrm{PA}^{-}$. An appendix further shows that $\mathrm{PA}^{-}_{\mathrm{jer}}+\mathrm{pa17}$ proves both the predecessor principle $\mathrm{pa14}$ and the subtraction principle $\mathrm{pa15}$.

papers.title: Constructions and reductions on the Hornich-Hlawka inequality and its generalizations
papers.abstract: We investigate five open problems concerning the Hornich-Hlawka inequality and its generalizations posed by Marinescu and Niculescu. We give constructive answers to three of them. First, we construct an equivalent norm on $\ell^2$ with no three-dimensional Hornich-Hlawka subspace. Second, we present a Nakano space that is not Hornich-Hlawka. Third, we show that the $α$-power generalization of the Hornich-Hlawka inequality fails to hold on nonzero normed spaces when $α\in (1, 2) \cup (2, \infty)$. This implies that on every nonzero inner product space, the $α$-power generalization of the Hornich-Hlawka inequality holds for all triples precisely when $α\in (0,1] \cup \{2\}$. For the remaining two problems, we establish reductions. We prove that $\ell^p(N)$ is Hornich-Hlawka for all $N \geq 3$ and $2 < p \leq \log 3 /(\log 3 - \log 2)$ if and only if it is Hornich-Hlawka at $N = 3$ and $p = \log 3 /(\log 3 - \log 2)$. Finally, for $p(\cdot): (0, 1) \to [1, 2]$ measurable and integers $k \geq 0$, we establish a Sobolev-Nakano equivalence: we prove that $W^{k,p(\cdot)}(0,1)$, equipped with the sum of the Luxemburg norms of its derivatives of orders $0, \ldots, k$, is Hornich-Hlawka if and only if $L^{p(\cdot)}(0,1)$ is Hornich-Hlawka.

papers.title: Diffusion-controlled reactions with time-dependent surface reactivity
papers.abstract: We investigate diffusion-controlled reactions on a reactive surface with time-dependent reactivity. Starting from a conventional formulation via diffusion equation with Robin boundary condition for the macroscopic concentration of particles, we aim at quantifying how temporal variations of reactivity affect the survival probability and the associated first-reaction time (FRT) of a single particle on the reactive surface. Using an adiabatic description, we first identify five long-time regimes of the first-reaction time distribution, ranging from exponential and stretched-exponential to power-law decay. In particular, sufficiently rapid decay of the reactivity leads to a nonzero probability of never reacting, despite diffusion in a bounded domain. Second, we provide a probabilistic reformulation of this problem and compare it with a different scenario of encounter-dependent reactivity. We use a heuristic mapping to compare the long-time kinetics of time-dependent and encounter-dependent reactivity. Our theoretical predictions are validated via extensive Monte Carlo simulations.

papers.title: Direct products of Gorenstein flat modules over coherent rings
papers.abstract: We construct a commutative coherent local algebra of Krull dimension zero and a countably generated projectively coresolved Gorenstein flat module whose countable power has infinite Gorenstein flat dimension. This answers negatively the question of whether Gorenstein flat modules over a right coherent ring are closed under direct products. As a consequence, we obtain a pure-injective Ding injective module whose character module has infinite Gorenstein flat dimension and whose character bidual has infinite Gorenstein injective dimension. We also give equivalent conditions for Gorenstein flat modules over a right coherent ring to be closed under direct products, in terms of relative Mittag--Leffler conditions, stationarity, and Gorenstein flat and injective dimensions of character biduals. For the constructed ring, we exhibit a decreasing countable sequence of strong submodules of a free module whose intersection has infinite Gorenstein flat dimension. Thus the abstract elementary class of Gorenstein flat modules, with the strong submodule relation, has finite character but does not admit intersections.

papers.title: On blow-up for the supercritical defocusing nonlinear scalar wave equation
papers.abstract: In this paper, we study finite-time singularity formation for the scalar defocusing nonlinear wave equation $-\partial_t^2u+Δu=u^p$. First, for fixed $d\geq4$ and odd $p\geq3$, we prove a conditional blow-up result under the assumption that the leading-order relativistic Euler system admits a smooth self-similar imploding profile whose associated normalized coefficients satisfy quantitative analytic radius conditions. Second, we verify both the existence of the profile and the analytic radius conditions in dimensions four and five for all sufficiently large odd $p$. Using the finite speed of propagation, we then obtain a threshold $p_0$, independent of the dimension, such that for every $d\geq4$ and every odd $p\geq p_0$, there exist smooth, compactly supported, real-valued initial data whose solutions blow up in finite time. The proof combines three ingredients: a normalized formulation that separates the leading periodic oscillation from the unknown modulation, the growth of the spatial analytic radius induced by an outgoing property, and frequency-dependent matrix multipliers that control the cumulative growth caused by the periodic linearized potential.

papers.title: Global Parameter Identification and Uncertainty Quantification of reduced-order ADM1 using Maximum Likelihood Estimation and Bayesian Inference
papers.abstract: Anaerobic digestion (AD) models can be challenging to calibrate against real data due to limited practical identifiability, data scarcity, and model complexity. Weighted least squares objective functions and gradient-based solvers using finite differences are often used in literature, but result in suboptimal parameter estimates and large uncertainty bands. This paper identifies the parameters of a reduced-order ADM1 by comparing the frameworks of maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) and Bayesian inference (BI), and quantifies uncertainties of parameters and outputs. Multirate experimental data are taken from a lab-scale AD reactor fed with agricultural substrates and operated at organic loading rates of 3$\,$g VS $\mathrm{m^{-3}d^{-1}}$. Global optima are found via global and gradient-based local search algorithms using forward sensitivities. Enhanced scatter search provides the best global search results. These are refined by the Gauss-Newton algorithm as the best local search, which delivers $R^2$ values of 0.95 for acetic acid and 0.77 for biogas production. BI yields substantially narrower uncertainty bands than MLE and avoids the need for a global search by incorporating prior knowledge about parameter distributions. The search space is captured efficiently by log10 scaling of parameters. Algorithmic details on its implications are provided. Despite a high-resolution lab-scale dataset, the ADM1-specific inhibition parameter $K_\mathrm{I,nh3}$ is practically not identifiable with MLE, and shows a low output sensitivity, whereas a parameter for the effective ion concentration shows superb practical identifiabilty at high confidence with both MLE and BI. The present work lays a scalable base for calibration of nonlinear AD models by providing reliable simulations. It thus advances model-based monitoring and control applications of multirate processes such as agricultural AD plants.

papers.title: Doubly commuting invariant and co-invariant subspaces
papers.abstract: Let $\mathcal{H}_{i}$ be complex separable Hilbert spaces and $T_{i}\in\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}_{i})$ for $i=1,\dots,n$. On the Hilbert tensor product $\mathfrak{H}:=\mathcal{H}_{1}\otimes\cdots\otimes\mathcal{H}_{n}$, consider the operator tuple $(\tilde{T}_{1},\dots,\tilde{T}_{n})$ defined by $T_{i}:=I_{\mathcal{H}_{1}}\otimes \cdots \otimes I_{\mathcal{H}_{i-1}}\otimes T_{i}\otimes I_{\mathcal{H}_{i+1}}\otimes \cdots \otimes I_{\mathcal{H}_{n}}.$ A closed jointly $(\tilde{T}_{1},\dots,\tilde{T}_{n})$-invariant subspace $\mathfrak{M}\subseteq\mathfrak{H}$ is doubly commuting if $(\tilde{T}_{1}\vert{}_{\mathfrak{M}},\dots,\tilde{T}_{n}\vert{}_{\mathfrak{M}})$ is doubly commuting. We prove that if the hereditary polynomials in each $T_{i}$ ($i=1,\dots,n$) are ultraweakly dense in $\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}_i)$, then $\mathfrak{M}$ is doubly commuting if and only if $\mathfrak{M}=\mathcal{M}_1\otimes\cdots\otimes\mathcal{M}_n$, where each $\mathcal{M}_i\subseteq\mathcal{H}_i$ is a closed $T_{i}$-invariant subspace. As applications, this provides a unified framework for characterizing doubly commuting quotient modules of weighted Bergman spaces over $\mathbb{D}^{n}$ and tensor products of complete Nevanlinna-Pick spaces. It also characterizes doubly commuting jointly invariant subspaces for tuples of backward shifts and their adjoints on tensor products of de Branges-Rovnyak spaces $H(b)$ (for both extreme and certain nonextreme $b$), as well as for tuples of coordinate Volterra operators and its adjoints on $L^2((0,1)^n;\mathbb{C})$. In particular cases, we recover known characterizations of doubly commuting quotient modules of $H^2(\mathbb{D}^n)$ and doubly commuting submodules of its Jordan blocks. Finally, our framework extends naturally to mixed tensor products combining distinct factor spaces from any of these settings.

papers.title: Holding Agents Accountable with Verifiable Agent Insurance
papers.abstract: While AI agents are useful for many tasks, they regularly misbehave in destructive ways, such as deleting important data. While prior work has focused on preventing such misbehavior, we consider how to recover after an agent misbehaves. We propose verifiable agent insurance (VAI), a framework for agent providers to commit financially to promises, a list of programmatically-specified policies that an agent is meant to follow. These promises are embedded in a smart contract on an immutable ledger (e.g., a blockchain) to prevent tampering, along with a monetary escrow. A user who detects a violation of committed promises can prompt a verifier to review agent execution traces, which are logged through the agent harness's shared tool-execution path, without instrumenting each tool separately. Upon verification of the violation, the agent provider's escrow funds are paid to the reporting user. We instantiate VAI as an end-to-end implementation on an Ethereum layer-2 network, and evaluate its coverage on three prominent agent benchmarks, two of which we re-annotated to obtain task-level policy-compliance labels. Currently, many agents do not emit user authorizations and security-relevant information as explicit, structured data objects -- rather, they embed the data needed to verify policy violations in natural language exchanges. Even so, VAI manages to detect violations in 63.6% of runs containing violations across three benchmarks. By augmenting agents to explicitly emit such objects, violation detection rises to 79.8% of runs containing violations. Our findings suggest that for improved auditability, agents should be co-designed with their security policies to emit explicit, structured records of user authorization and security-relevant actions.

papers.title: Towards the Geometry of Quantum Optical Measurements: Kraus Trajectories in the Instrumental Weyl-Heisenberg Group Manifold
papers.abstract: Since ancient Greek times, geometry has been a method by which humans can make inferences, by the use of similar triangles, about the world far beyond their immediate senses. Similarity plays an equally important role in quantum measurement, except that instead of between triangles on wax tablets and in the sky, the similarity is between the infinitesimal generators of transformation (i.e. rotation, affine canonical transformation) on the page and within the atom. For many quantum optical measurements of a single mode, these generators produce Kraus operators that are contained within a twelve-dimensional Lie group: the Instrumental Weyl-Heisenberg group manifold ($\mathrm{IWH}^{\textbf{12}}$). In particular, $\mathrm{IWH}^{\textbf{12}}$ is general enough to include all diffusively generated 'dyne measurements. In this paper, $\mathrm{IWH}^{\textbf{12}}$ will be used to develop two more general classes of 'dyne measurement: one that interpolates between diffusive homodyne and diffusive heterodyne (``slomodyne'') and one that adds to 'dyne measurements adaptive squeezing and displacement. Our analysis uses an approach known as the Instrument Manifold Program (IMP). In particular, a Harish-Chandra-like decomposition of $\mathrm{IWH}^{\textbf{12}}$ is used to calculate the vielbein transformation from a right-invariant basis to the corresponding coordinate basis, allowing us to universally and autonomously navigate $\mathrm{IWH}^{\textbf{12}}$ and locate the Kraus-operator of whatever selective process is being considered as it evolves in time according to the measurement record.

papers.title: Linear Demand Systems are Consistent with Discrete Choice
papers.abstract: Aggregate linear demand systems can be micro-founded by a population of heterogeneous consumers making discrete choices. They can also be extended to incorporate income effects. I prove these results and show how to structurally estimate this class of models using only market-level data. The distribution of heterogeneous consumer preferences is recovered by disciplining the corner solutions with aggregate terms only. This approach allows for the same richness of Berry, Levinsohn, and Pakes (1995) [BLP] while retaining the analytical and computational advantages of linear demand: it does not require exogenously fixing market size, allows for heterogeneity in choice sets, and results in a flexible substitution matrix which varies endogenously as different consumers enter/exit the market. The discrete-choice microfoundation facilitates welfare analysis and the flexible measurement of markups an cost pass-throughs, among a wide range of other applications.

papers.title: Learning Representations to Guide Pixel Diffusion Transformers
papers.abstract: Visual representations are largely developed for understanding, yet what makes them useful for generation remains unclear. We study this question in pixel diffusion transformers and uncover two key insights. First, better representation quality does not necessarily translate into greater generative utility, as externally aligned semantics can be progressively lost during pixel synthesis. Second, architectural separation with specialized pixel decoders mainly redistributes semantic and spatial modeling, without necessarily yielding representations better suited to generation. These insights suggest that a useful generative representation must be both properly formed and actively exploited. Motivated by these insights, we introduce Representation Guidance (RG), which directly forms and exploits internal representations while retaining a plain Transformer architecture. A low-dimensional bottleneck forces generation-relevant information into a compact representation, which is then explicitly used to guide decoder generation by modifying the flow-matching target according to its induced prediction offset. RG learns clearer semantic and spatial structure while scaling efficiently in both parameters and computation. On ImageNet 256x256, RG-L/16 with only 459M parameters outperforms substantially larger pixel diffusion transformers, while RG-XL/16 achieves an FID of 1.55. RG further reaches an FID of 1.74 at 512x512 and extends to text-to-image generation, achieving 0.89 on GenEval and 87.1 on DPG-Bench.

papers.title: Nonminimizing Attration of Stochastic Subgradient Methods on Semialgebraic Functions
papers.abstract: We construct a globally Lipschitz, coercive, semialgebraic function in two dimensions for which stochastic subgradient iterates converge to the origin, a Clarke critical point that is neither limiting critical nor a local minimizer. For power-law stepsizes, this attraction holds on open sets of initial points and linear tilts, uniformly over all noise sequences within a prescribed bound. The example shows that subdifferential regularity cannot be removed from the generic guarantee of convergence to local minimizers established by Davis, Drusvyatskiy, and Jiang (2026). For the same tilted objectives and initial points, the unique Clarke subgradient flow converges to a strict local minimizer. Thus, convergence of continuous-time flows to local minimizers cannot by itself justify the corresponding guarantee for discrete subgradient methods, even with diminishing stepsizes.

papers.title: Fourier Restriction Beyond Dimension Data: A Multiscale Moment Criterion
papers.abstract: We establish an exact restriction criterion for weighted Moran measures with uniformly bounded one-level frame bounds: for every $2<s<\infty$, $L^2(μ)\to L^s(\mathbb R)$ extension holds if and only if $\widehatμ\in L^s(\mathbb R)$, equivalently, if and only if $\sum_nG_{s,n}<\infty$, where $G_{s,n}$ sums the $s$th powers of the magnitudes of the $n$th digit mask at its nonzero grid frequencies. The proof combines finite-frame stability and multiscale iteration with disjoint resonant frequency grids. The criterion determines the critical restriction exponent and characterizes its attainment when it lies in $(1,2)$. We construct singular continuous spectral Moran measures with common scales, digit cardinalities, exponential spectrum, maximal mask magnitudes at nonzero grid frequencies, and a global Fourier decay bound sharp along a common resonant sequence, yet different critical restriction exponents. For any prescribed finite positive summability exponent of these maxima, we determine the optimal interval of critical restriction exponents and realize both endpoint attainment and failure at every interior point with the same fixed data. These measures can simultaneously satisfy $\dim_{\mathrm F}^θμ=θ$ for $0\leθ\le1$ and $D_q(μ)=1$ for $1<q\le\infty$, with local dimension one at every support point. Finite-field spectral constructions realize every critical restriction exponent in $[1,2]$ with these dimensional data and exhibit sharp logarithmic endpoint transitions. They also yield singular continuous measures with Fourier dimension zero, restriction for all $1\le p<2$, and stretched-logarithmic Fourier decay with an optimal exponent. Finally, all-scale $L^q$-dimension formulas yield explicit examples where dimensional criteria strictly improve the classical Stein--Tomas--Mockenhaupt range.

papers.title: Refine Connections, Close the Gap: A Reliable Enhancement Framework for Driving Scene Topology
papers.abstract: In autonomous driving, understanding scene topology -- the connectivity between lanes and traffic elements -- is critical for safe path planning and motion control. While current methods excel at detecting individual map elements, their connectivity reasoning often falls short of its theoretical potential, leaving a significant performance gap relative to the theoretical upper-bound (Oracle) achievable given the underlying detections. To bridge this gap, we propose TopoEnhance, a novel topology enhancement framework designed to unlock the latent potential of existing methods by refining their connectivity predictions. We formulate topology enhancement as a denoising-based reconstruction process, where the model learns to recover structural consistency from stochastically corrupted ground-truth graphs. This training strategy does not require predictions from upstream topology models. Experiments on OpenLane-V2 show that TopoEnhance consistently improves $TOP_{ll}$ and $TOP_{lt}$ across diverse prediction sources, narrowing the gap to the detection-conditioned Upper-Bound without source-specific retraining. Further evaluations demonstrate improvements in ego-route recoverability, downstream trajectory prediction, and temporal consistency.

papers.title: Non-degeneracy and Fibering with Applications to Diophantine Approximation
papers.abstract: Motivated by applications in Diophantine approximation, we develop a new fibering mechanism for non-degenerate manifolds in $\mathbb{R}^n$, showing that they admit local decompositions into families of non-degenerate curves with uniform quantitative non-degeneracy estimates. Our construction applies to $l$ non-degenerate $C^N$ manifolds under the optimal regularity assumption $N\geq\max\{n,l\}$, requiring no additional smoothness. Furthermore, we show that this uniform quantitative local control can be globalised into a qualitative statement, so that almost every point of a non-degenerate manifold lies on a non-degenerate curve contained in the manifold. The resulting quantitative fibering estimates are also stable under sufficiently small $C^n$ perturbations at each fixed spatial scale. The method provides a framework for extending fibering based results in Diophantine approximation from curves to manifolds. Such applications are considered in the paper.

papers.title: LLM Persuasion Is in the Eye of the Evaluation
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have already been shown to match or exceed human experts in persuasion. While their persuasive capabilities hold promise for beneficial uses such as education and health communication, they can also be used to manipulate and misinform, making their evaluation a growing priority for developers and regulators. That evaluation, however, remains fragmented: studies differ in what they treat as persuasion, and broad claims often rest on narrow, situation-specific assessments. Automated methods, often modelled on human studies, offer a way to compare such assessments directly, as they can be run on the same models at scale and can include high-risk forms of persuasion that would be difficult or unethical to test on people. In this study, we adapt nine published automated methods to a shared setup, run them on the same fifteen LLMs, and ask whether their rankings agree and why. We find that the methods agree only weakly (mean Spearman $ρ= 0.25$). Our analyses point to two contributing factors. Models that refuse some tasks but not others, directly or indirectly, lower agreement by about a quarter, and these refusals fall mostly on manipulation tasks. General capability also plays a part: most rational persuasion (non-manipulative) methods track it, whereas most manipulation methods do not. Together, these findings suggest that agreement depends more on the task a method sets than on how it scores persuasion, although this pattern is only indicative given the eight methods available for analysis. More broadly, our results suggest that persuasion scores combine a model's ability to persuade with its willingness to do so. A single score is therefore informative about its own setting, but says little about a model's persuasiveness across tasks.

papers.title: A Single-Loop, Constant-Batch First-Order Penalty Method for Stochastic Bilevel Optimization
papers.abstract: Recent advances in penalty-based methods for stochastic bilevel optimization (SBO) have eliminated the need for second-order derivative oracles. However, for stochastic nonconvex-strongly convex bilevel problems, existing first-order methods typically rely on nested loops and/or large batch sizes for attaining $O(ε^{-6})$ or $O(ε^{-4})$ sample complexity under standard bounded-variance assumption or mean-square smoothness assumption. Achieving these rates with a single-loop penalty method and a constant batch size remains challenging due to a large penalty value needed for an accurate approximation. To address this challenge, we develop a stochastic SIngle-loop COnstant-Batch first-order penalty method (SICO) that combines two complementary ingredients. First, it performs one stochastic-gradient update per-iteration for both the original lower-level and penalized problems, with a projection that controls the separation between their iterates. Second, it applies an exponential moving average to stabilize the upper-level gradient estimator. We show that this combination achieves $ O(ε^{-6}) $ sample complexity using only $O(1)$ stochastic-gradient samples per iteration under unbiased, bounded-variance stochastic gradients. Under the additional mean-square smoothness assumption on the lower-level stochastic gradients, the same algorithm improves the complexity to $O(ε^{-4})$ also with $O(1)$ batch size. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to match the best-known convergence rate for fully first-order SBO methods using a single loop and a constant batch size. This result addresses an open problem posed in the literature.

papers.title: Propagation and horizon formation in Einstein--Gauss--Bonnet scalar collapse. I. Characteristic conditions, bounds and formation
papers.abstract: We study scalar collapse in five- and six-dimensional Einstein--Gauss--Bonnet gravity with positive coupling as an exact classical theory. On spherical scalar backgrounds, gravitational characteristic conditions reduce to inequalities in two local invariants. In five dimensions, they imply $R_h^2>\tildeα$ for regular marginal spheres on the GR branch and the sharp Kretschmann bound $\tildeα^2\mathcal R_{abcd}\mathcal R^{abcd}<28$ for nonnegative mass. Under the stated finite-domain hypotheses, spherical continuation places the first characteristic degeneration on a smooth background. Within this setting, a future marginal sphere formed while the characteristic conditions hold throughout the preceding evolution forces their later failure. For every allowed radius, separately chosen complete smooth data form marginal spheres with mass arbitrarily close to the sharp lower bound; in six dimensions both radius and mass can be arbitrarily small. At sufficiently large scale, complete nonspherical data with weak curvature contain marginal surfaces with prescribed $S^3$ metrics under a spectral condition. These surfaces are outermost and strictly stable. A separate Berger family has arbitrarily small area at one common ADM mass; formation from untrapped data remains open. Exact nonspherical developments have smoothly convergent initial data but tidal tensors that fail to converge to the reference values at a chosen time after the reference core loses hyperbolicity. Under local geometric uniqueness for developments of the same data on overlaps connecting the initial slice to the observers, classical existence on a common region and continuous dependence of the tidal tensor cannot both hold. The constructed solutions themselves extend smoothly. Fixed time averages converge on the controlled interval, but this does not establish a predictive effective-field-theory continuation.

papers.title: Direction-Conditioned Policies for Online Goal-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Contrastive Reinforcement Learning (CRL) learns representations that estimate goal reachability, yet its policy remains conditioned on raw goals and therefore does not directly exploit the geometry encoded by its critic. We introduce Direction-Conditioned Policies (DCP), a method built around a small modification to CRL: DCP selects previously visited states as waypoints during online training and conditions the policy on their direction and distance in representation space. At deployment, DCP applies the same interface directly to the final goal, requiring neither waypoint selection nor planning. Across nine navigation and manipulation tasks, DCP attains higher final success rates than CRL on seven tasks and spends more time near the goal on seven. Ablations show that most of the gains come from conditioning on direction and distance, while the waypoints let DCP learn on every task, including those where the goal is rarely reached early in training. Controlled maze experiments further show that DCP captures shortest-path geometry more accurately and that the supplied direction causally influences the actor's behavior. Finally, we show that learned candidate generation improves goal reaching in two controlled mazes.

papers.title: Salvation Lies Within: Eliciting Inherent Style Transfer in Step-Distilled Diffusion Models
papers.abstract: Adapting step-distilled text-to-image (T2I) models through post-training incurs additional computational costs and affects native few-step generation behavior. This motivates a complementary route beyond style-specific adaptation: drawing on the visual knowledge already encoded in step-distilled T2I models to elicit stylistic capabilities through language. Pursuing this direction requires textual guidance that captures how visual attributes jointly define a style and remain applicable as the depicted content changes. To explore this approach, we introduce StyleForge, a fully automatic, training-free framework that expresses reference styles as reusable rendering instructions. By integrating overall rendering characteristics with local color and lighting behavior, StyleForge organizes visual evidence from reference images into a coherent specification of how the target style should be expressed. The specification is then compiled into textual guidance that can be reused across content prompts, enabling frozen step-distilled T2I models to render different subjects and scenes in the reference style while retaining native few-step generation. Extensive experiments show relative gains of up to 29.47\% in generation quality scores over the strongest baseline, while Pareto analysis indicates that improved stylization is accompanied by strong adherence to the requested content. Code is available at https://github.com/sunshy-1/StyleForge.

papers.title: RouteAudit: A Negative Result on Adaptive Multi-Verifier Routing under Matched Fixed-Subset Controls
papers.abstract: Apparent savings from adaptive verifier routing can come from a fixed verifier subset. We audit GSM8K using cached Qwen3.5-0.8B or Qwen3.5-2B candidates paired with Qwen3-4B, three LLM verifiers, 1,319 held-out requests, and 5 router seeds. Our shared-fusion audit compares routers with the complete fixed-subset envelope, including zero-call abstention, under matched prices and scoring. Calibration-selected single-call verification matches full static verification in 3 of 4 cells. In a separate comparison using the original fusion rules and two-verifier catalog, archived learned and offline-RL routers lose 0.038 to 0.171 in quality against matched static SF+SA. Across 480 budget-matched offline fits in six router families, the family envelope gain is zero in each cell at the primary price. No locked router obtains a positive simultaneous bootstrap lower bound across 68 cell-by-price points. None is classified as complete-static dominant, and all 4 primary-price points are inconclusive. At the primary price, the tested-family gain upper bound is at most 0.002. The oracle headroom upper bound is 0.034 to 0.045, above our 0.01 margin, leaving meaningful gains open. At 45 of 64 grid points excluding the primary price, the oracle lower bound exceeds 0.01 and the tested-family upper bound is at most 0.01. Coverage of these envelope bounds remains unverified. At a true gain of 0.03, the procedure rejects on 44.1% of points, and planted-effect family coverage ranges from 0.923 to 0.931. We report lessons from this catalog.

papers.title: FAER: A Negative-Result Audit of Offline Trajectory Replay Selection on GSM8K
papers.abstract: Offline trajectory replay selects model-generated reasoning traces from a frozen cache for supervised fine-tuning (SFT), yet cache-side answer correctness need not predict downstream accuracy on unseen problems. We report a failure-retaining audit of offline response SFT on GSM8K with Qwen3-1.7B fp16 LoRA over a frozen 384-row cache (256 training rows and 128 excluded held-out rows). Across three seeds (13, 17, 23) on a 256-problem test split, all three 32-row replay rules (uniform, format-feedback, and feedback-aware) obtain mean strict accuracies (0.7786, 0.7682, and 0.7956) below the no-update base model (0.8008), and every paired 95% confidence interval spans zero. Selector ranking is post-hoc unidentified (3 completed selectors versus the repaired protocol's minimum of 5, with rank correlation spanning both signs). Under an 8,192-supervised-token windowed schedule, 9 of 12 runs halt under calibration drift or unresolved nonfinite training loss or gradients, leaving only full-cache replay completed at 0.7721. A repaired campaign with dynamic loss scaling halted at its learning-rate pilot under reference-solution loss drift before accessing the 346-problem locked test split. Because the gold-rationale positive control was never executed, these negative results cannot separate cache quality, selector quality, and learner-protocol limits. Our one positive finding separates parser repair from prompt changes on a 64-problem audit split: reparsing fixed base generations with a Decimal extractor raises parse rate from 0.8750 to 1.0000 and accuracy from 0.7344 to 0.8281, whereas appending a format suffix flips 0.2500 of canonical answers. A preregistered replication on 512 fresh GSM8K training problems reproduces this parser-only gain (+8.40 pp, 95% CI [+6.05, +10.94]) for this checkpoint. We contribute a ledger-traceable negative-result record and 9 lessons learned.

papers.title: Montesinos Knots with Delta-Unknotting Number One
papers.abstract: The $Δ$-unknotting number for a knot is defined as the minimum number of $Δ$-moves needed to deform the knot into the trivial knot. In this paper, we discuss Montesinos knots whose $Δ$-unknotting number is equal to one. We propose a conjectural characterization of Montesinos knots with $Δ$-unknotting number one and provide examples admitting distinct $Δ$-moves, each of which deforms the knot into the trivial knot. Furthermore, we present examples illustrating the relationship between the locations of $Δ$-moves and $X$-moves for knots with $u^Δ(K) = 1$, considering separately the cases $u(K) = 1$ and $u(K) = 2$.

papers.title: Finite-momentum trimers and Cooper quartets in a one-dimensional Fermi gas with coexistent $s$- and $p$-wave interactions
papers.abstract: We study finite-momentum trimers and Cooper quartets in a one-dimensional two-component Fermi gas with coexistent $s$- and $p$-wave interactions, regularized in the relative momentum of each pair so that they remain Galilean invariant. Pauli blocking alone then makes the trimer dispersion deviate from free center-of-mass motion, so the trimer energy can be lowest at finite total momentum. Allowing this motion expands the $abb$ region among pairs and trimers and removes the region where an odd-wave pair is lowest. The $aabb$ quartet lies below all these branches at every sampled coupling, and in a strip starting on the crossing of the two dimer-pair channels its lowest breakup channel is a moving $abb$ trimer and an atom. At weak interspecies attraction, a variational bound shows that two odd-wave Cooper pairs bind into a quartet, whose binding exceeds that of the coexisting trimer by orders of magnitude as the attraction weakens. At stronger interspecies attraction, the quartet binding relative to two unlike-species dimers disappears when the odd-wave interaction is switched off, although the even-wave interaction dominates the interaction energy. Relative to the in-vacuum case, the Fermi sea enhances the weak-coupling quartet binding, and at fixed scattering lengths the quartet binding grows with density while the coexisting trimer becomes much shallower. These results show that neither the most strongly bound pair nor the dominant interaction energy alone determines whether the quartet binds.

papers.title: Transverse momentum as the counter-diabatic generator in bent waveguide couplers
papers.abstract: Axis bending of a mode-evolution coupler realizes the counter-diabatic (CD) protocol [Opt. Express 34, 1214 (2026)]. We identify the operator responsible. Rigid lateral displacement is generated by the transverse momentum $\hat p_x$, which in a real two-mode supermode basis is purely $σ_y$: exactly the form of the CD term, and the one form that detuning and coupling cannot supply. Equating the two gives the axis slope in closed form, as a ratio of two matrix elements at a single cross section, or $\dot{x}_0=\dotθ/(γΔβ^{2})$ in coupled-mode variables. It agrees with a numerical offset search to 0.3% and is shown to be the earlier curvature condition viewed from the Kramers-Henneberger frame. Beam propagation simulations compare the bent coupler directly with the unitary-transformation realization built from the same reference structure: the two reach supermode fidelities of 0.994 and 1.000 against 0.886 for the untreated coupler, show comparable bandwidth and fabrication tolerance, and differ inside the device by the frame transformation that relates them.

papers.title: Sparse-View Interpretable 3D Animal Behavior Representations for Neural Encoding and Decoding
papers.abstract: A deeper understanding of brain function requires a precise, structured characterization of behavior. Yet, extracting behavioral representations from video in a form suitable for scientific analysis remains a fundamental challenge. Many prior studies represent behavior via pose estimation or nonlinear video embeddings. However, pose tracking discards rich information beyond predefined keypoints, while nonlinear video embeddings lack interpretability. We address this limitation with SABLE (Sparse-view Animal Behavior Latent Embeddings), a self-supervised framework that leverages a geometric inductive bias to learn behavior representations. By augmenting a multi-view transformer with priors from monocular depth and pose estimation, SABLE reconstructs 3D animal behavior from extremely sparse views while learning explicit 3D latent structure. Without ground-truth 3D labels, it reliably recovers 3D behavior from two-view videos, whereas state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods fail or yield degenerate solutions. Across the International Brain Lab and Cheese3D datasets, we demonstrate that SABLE learns 3D representations that match or exceed prior SOTA performance in neural encoding and decoding. Single-neuron analyses further identify neurons with putative 3D tuning, generating testable hypotheses about how the brain represents 3D behavior. Once pretrained across animals, SABLE serves as an off-the-shelf model that generalizes zero-shot to unseen animals without animal-specific calibration or retraining. Our method establishes 3D-aware video embeddings that capture complex behavior, opening new avenues for studying brain-behavior relationships.

papers.title: Language Models Act on Hidden Valence
papers.abstract: Language models describe some internal states as good and others as bad. But whether models have a stake in them is an open question. Simply asking models is unlikely to be informative. Any answer may be consistent with genuine introspection, superficial pattern-matching, or with fixed scripts learned in character training. We therefore study revealed preference. Rather than asking about a state, we use activation steering to attach a positively or negatively valenced activation pattern to one of two otherwise meaningless 'zones', switch steering off, and then observe which zone the model prefers. A model with a stake in that state should choose accordingly. Across seven open-weight models from five families, this is indeed what we find. First, steering changes the passages models write about each zone, and those words shift later choice. Second, this shift persists when all surface-level tokens are held fixed and only the hidden KV cache differs. Third, the effect also remains when all text is generated without steering and valence is only injected during cache construction. Thus, the hidden state is sufficient to move choice in proportion to the steering dose. Fourth, the dependence of choice on hidden valence is nearly absent in a base model and emerges during DPO, consistent with a link between valence and goal-directed behaviour formed in training. Finally, given tools to self-steer, a model does not tend to induce a positive state, but it regularly removes an imposed negative state. It does so at a dose-dependent rate and significantly more often than it removes random-direction interventions. Overall we demonstrate that valence-related activation patterns leave hidden traces that predictably govern later choices, even when all visible tokens are identical across conditions. Whether these traces are accompanied by any subjective experience relevant to model welfare remains unclear.

papers.title: Muon Sublates the Edge of Stability in LLM Pretraining: What Persists and What Changes
papers.abstract: Muon is increasingly used for language-model pretraining, yet its large-step dynamics are not captured by the classical edge-of-stability (EoS) picture of gradient descent (GD). We study stochastic (no-momentum) Muon through theoretical analysis, controlled networks, and language models from 22M to 1B parameters, distinguishing three diagnostics: generalized sharpness, loss balance, and update alignment. We theoretically and empirically demonstrate that loss balance differs from its generalized sharpness and cannot determine update alignment across various learning rates in 130M pre-training as well as 1B runs. Besides, our experiments also show that increasing the batch size encourages update alignment towards to total reversal. Furthermore, checkpoint interventions in the 22M and 130M models show that increasing the learning rate can initially raise the loss but a lower validation loss at the end of the prescribed warmup-stable-decay continuation. These results support a split EoS picture: generalized-sharpness saturation persists in the measured runs, but loss balance and update geometry require separate characterization, allowing for learning-rate schedules design. The source code for reproducing the experiments can be found in https://github.com/cyzebra/Muon-Sublates-the-Edge-of-Stability-in-LLM-Pretraining.

papers.title: Asymptotically Hölder gradient regularity for degenerate or singular parabolic normalized $ p$-Laplace equations
papers.abstract: We study bounded viscosity solutions of the degenerate or singular parabolic equation \[ u_t-|Du|^γΔ_p^{\mathrm{N}}u=f \qquad \text{in } Q_1, \] where \[ Δ_p^{\mathrm{N}}u := Δu+(p-2) \left\langle D^2u\frac{Du}{|Du|}, \frac{Du}{|Du|} \right\rangle, \qquad -1<γ<\infty,\quad 1<p<\infty, \] and $f\in C^0(Q_1)\cap L^\infty(Q_1)$. Given any prescribed $α\in(0,1)$, we prove that there exists $\varepsilon=\varepsilon(n,α)>0$ such that \[ |p-2|+|γ|\leq\varepsilon \quad\Longrightarrow\quad u\in C_{\mathrm{loc}}^{1+α,\frac{1+α}{2}}(Q_1). \] In particular, the spatial gradient Hölder exponent can be chosen arbitrarily close to $ 1 $ as $(p,γ)\to(2,0)$. This extends the result of Andrade and Santos (Calc. Var. Partial Differential Equations \textbf{61}, Paper No. 196, 2022) for $γ=0$ to the joint regime $(p,γ)\to(2,0)$ and answers affirmatively the question raised in Remark~1.1 therein.

papers.title: Long Time No See: Benchmarking VLMs for Out-of-Sight Spatiotemporal Reasoning in Egocentric Videos
papers.abstract: Real-world AI systems must reason about objects that are no longer visible: an AR assistant guiding a user back to an object used earlier, a household robot retrieving an item someone put away. This requires not just recalling where an object was last seen, but updating its state when it is moved and retaining that update once it leaves view. We refer to this as out-of-sight spatiotemporal reasoning. We introduce Beyond3D, the first VQA benchmark to isolate this ability in dynamic egocentric video: every query targets an object that has been relocated and has since left the field of view. We create our questions from HD-EPIC annotations, building a visibility track for each dynamic object from its 3D position, the camera pose, and the scene geometry to understand at each moment whether it is visible, occluded, or out of view. Beyond3D comprises 9,000 questions in eight types over 135 videos from nine participants, organized as one reasoning chain: visual grounding (is the target observable now), temporal grounding (when it was last visible and last placed), scene localization (which fixture anchors that location), and 3D spatial perception (where it lies relative to the current viewpoint or another object in the scene). We benchmark nine general-purpose and spatially specialized VLMs. The best model reaches 42.2% against 29.7% chance and text-only baselines reaching 31.9%, with the largest failures in recovering when an object was last visible, showing that tracking object movement out of sight remains far from solved for current VLMs.

papers.title: Beyond End-to-End Black-Box Mapping: An Intentional Agent Framework for Cognitively Driven Facial Reaction Generation
papers.abstract: In dyadic human-human interactions, a listener's facial reactions reflect latent states containing memories of earlier interactions, thoughts, emotions, and expectations. However, many facial reaction generation (FRG) methods predict reactions from speaker behaviour and interaction history without explicitly modelling these factors or connecting ongoing interpretation with latent state evolution and facial feedback. We introduce the Intentional Facial Reaction Generation Agent (IFRGA), which uses an explicit latent state to connect interaction interpretation with facial reaction generation. Its Latent State Evolution Module (LSEM) updates this state using relevant memory, retained thoughts, and current speaker behaviour through a computational mechanism inspired by human thought processes. Within LSEM, the Inner Thought Flow (ITF) carries thoughts across updates, allowing interpretations to build on earlier thoughts while incorporating current behaviour. This supports real-time, proactive inference. The Facial Reaction Generation Module (FRGM) aligns current thoughts, emotion values, and available speaker behaviour over time. It combines predicted facial values with changes generated by a Diffusion Transformer to produce reactions guided by both speaker behaviour and latent state evolution. On REACT 2025, IFRGA achieves a correlation score of 0.8367 and a distance score of 143.64 against reference reactions, numerically outperforming published results of compared learnt methods. A blinded human evaluation shows that carrying thoughts across matched updates significantly improves naturalness and contextual appropriateness compared with carrying factual summaries.

papers.title: From Hidden States to Stated Confidence: Self-Distillation for Reasoning Models
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with binary correctness rewards trains correctness, not calibrated confidence. The confidence that reasoning models verbalize is overconfident and tracks how willing a model is to commit to an answer rather than how likely the answer is to be right, so post-hoc rescaling rarely transfers. We look inside the model instead. On factual question answering, a linear probe on the hidden state between the chain of thought and the answer has 5-38x lower expected calibration error (ECE) than the verbalized score across four benchmarks and two model families. Since a probe needs hidden-state access, we introduce probe-guided self-distillation (Probe-SD): the probe scores the model's own sampled traces, each trace's stated confidence is overwritten with that score, and the base checkpoint is finetuned on the result, so the model itself states calibrated confidence at test time. On Qwen3-14B, Probe-SD cuts out-of-domain ECE from 0.542 to 0.113, beats post-hoc recalibration and self-distillation with sample-based labels, and keeps the confidence stated while reasoning consistent with the final score. Its question-level variant, Probe-SD-Q, lowers ECE further to 0.099, and the gains carry over to multiple-choice QA with shuffled options. The probe mainly separates questions the model knows from those it does not. As an answer selector it nearly ties majority voting, so we use it as a confidence, not a selector.

papers.title: ASSEMBLE: Atomic Skills for Evidence-Grounded Video Reasoning
papers.abstract: Complex video reasoning often depends on evidence scattered across distant moments, entities, and events, yet a correct answer alone does not reveal whether a model relied on the right parts of the video. We introduce ASSEMBLE, a framework that makes supporting evidence explicit throughout long-video reasoning. It organizes local observations and cross-clip narratives into timestamped evidence catalogs traceable to the source video. A grounding-aware reader then composes question-specific atomic skills whose structured outputs include explicit evidence references and support assessments. Following teacher-supervised fine-tuning, we train the reader with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) using answer correctness and correctness-gated citation alignment. The resulting reasoning traces are inspectable, and final predictions remain linked to explicit supporting evidence. With a 9B reader supervised by a 235B teacher and shared precomputed evidence catalogs, ASSEMBLE achieves 59.2% macro-averaged answer accuracy across three long-video reasoning benchmarks, compared with 58.3% for Gemini-2.5-Pro, while improving macro-averaged overlap-based Grounded accuracy by 6.7 percentage points, with gains on all three benchmarks. Ablations show that, under the same post-trained reader and inference budget, structured skill inference improves overlap-based Grounded accuracy over free-form reasoning. Compared with generic structured reasoning, the benefit is more setting-dependent, with the clearest answer-accuracy gain on VRBench. These results show that explicit evidence grounding can improve long-video reasoning while keeping predictions tied to their supporting evidence.

papers.title: The maximum number of edges in minimal matching covered graphs
papers.abstract: A connected graph $G$ with at least two vertices is {\em matching covered} if each of its edges lies in a perfect matching. A matching covered graph is {\em minimal} if the removal of any edge results in a graph that is no longer matching covered. Lovász and Plummer [J. Combin. Theory, Ser. B 23 (1977) 127--138] proved by ear decompositions that every minimal matching covered bipartite graph $G$ with at least 6 vertices has at most $(3|V(G)|-6)/2$ edges, and this bound is sharp for all even $|V(G)|\ge6$. Very recently, Mallik, Diwan and Kothari [J. Combin. 17 (4) (2026) 559--606] determined the extremal graphs achieving this upper bound. In this paper, we prove that every minimal matching covered nonbipartite graph $G$ with at least 6 vertices has at most $(5|V(G)|-10)/2$ edges. Moreover, we show that if $G$ is not bicritical, then $G$ has at most $(5|V(G)|-14)/2$ edges and if $G$ is 3-connected and has at least 14 vertices, then $G$ has at most $(5|V(G)|-26)/2$ edges. All three bounds are sharp, and all the corresponding extremal graphs are characterized.

papers.title: The Sequential Price of Continual Learning
papers.abstract: Sequential task updates are fundamental to continual learning, but their recency bias can impose a lasting performance cost. We study this cost in an overparameterized linear-regression model with i.i.d. task sampling. We prove that distribution-level forgetting and population loss converge to the same stationary limit. We quantify the additional loss incurred by sequential exact fitting, or the sequential price. If all nonzero eigenvalues of all task curvature matrices equal the same constant, the stationary loss is exactly twice the joint-training optimum. We further analyze fixed-strength elastic weight consolidation (EWC) under general task curvatures and characterize its stationary sequential price at every regularization strength. Under strong regularization, the price decays inversely with EWC strength while the number of tasks sufficient to reduce the mean-square effect of initialization by a fixed factor grows proportionally. Real Jester user ratings, with a natural encoding and training procedure, satisfy our theoretical assumptions.

papers.title: Measuring Dual-Superconductor Length Scales in the QCD Vacuum at HERA
papers.abstract: In the dual-superconductor picture, the QCD vacuum behaves like a superconductor for chromoelectric fields, with characteristic penetration and coherence lengths. These scales have so far been studied primarily through lattice calculations of static flux tubes. We show that they are also imprinted on exclusive diffraction, where the transverse profile of a gluonic hotspot reflects the response of the vacuum to a localised colour source. Using the Clem vortex profile, we fit all 104 H1 and ZEUS measurements of exclusive $J/ψ$ photoproduction and find $χ^2/{\rm ndf}=0.72$, the penetration depth $λ=0.19(2)~{\rm fm}$, the hotspot core size $ξ_v=0.087(14)~{\rm fm}$, and the Ginzburg--Landau parameter $κ=2.6(8)$, placing the effective vacuum description in the type-II regime. The corresponding vector mass $1/λ=1.03(11)~{\rm GeV}$ agrees with the lattice gluelump mass, and the extracted parameters reproduce the QCD string tension.

papers.title: Towards Accurate Prediction of Mutation-Induced Changes in Protein Structure
papers.abstract: Proteins can possess numerous mutations relative to their wild-type amino acid sequences with minimal impact to their structure and function. However, in other cases, even a single amino acid mutation relative to the wild-type sequence can lead to a large change in structure or even a disease phenotype. While the accuracy of wild-type protein structure prediction has improved significantly in recent years, it remains difficult to accurately predict the structure of mutant proteins. Here, we characterize the local mutation-induced structural changes in proteins for a dataset of wildtype and the corresponding single-amino acid mutant x-ray crystal structures from the Protein Data Bank (PDB). We find that mutation-induced structural changes in these proteins are localized at the site of the mutation, decaying rapidly with increasing spatial distance from the mutation site. In addition, we evaluate how well AlphaFold3 can recapitulate the observed mutation-induced structural deformations in the x-ray crystal structures. We find that the accuracy of the AlphaFold3 predictions decreases strongly with increasing mutation-induced deformation. In contrast to the results for AlphaFold3, the Pearson correlation between a single physical feature, i.e. the change in solvent accessibility, and the mutation-induced deformation does not depend on the magnitude of the deformation. Our results and analyses provide a framework for further studies aimed at predicting the structural changes in proteins caused by single amino acid mutations.

papers.title: Optimal Allocation of Grid-Forming Frequency Shaping Control
papers.abstract: Various inverter-based control strategies have been proposed to improve frequency security for power systems with high renewable penetration. Among them, the grid-forming frequency shaping control is particularly promising due to its ability to shape the post-contingency aggregate system frequency dynamics into first-order with prescribed rate of change of frequency (RoCoF) and steady-state frequency deviation. Moreover, the shaped aggregate dynamics depends on the harmonic sum of all inverter transfer functions rather than on their distribution. In light of this, here we explore how to allocate shaping control resources to minimize the transient control effort needed to achieve ideal coherent dynamics. We formulate it as a constrained optimization problem by tackling two main difficulties. First, we make the squared $\mathcal{H}_2$ norm legitimate quantification of transient control cost under step power imbalances through a system transformation. Second, we simplify the $s$-domain constraint for Nadir elimination into a standard constraint that is easy to implement in optimization. The resulting non-convex optimization problem can be solved by existing successive convexification method. The effectiveness of the allocation has been verified on the modified Icelandic Power Network test case.

papers.title: Advanced 400G-SerDes Modulations and Equalizers for GPU Cluster in AI Era
papers.abstract: High-speed GPU cluster interconnects are evolving from 200 to 400 Gbps to meet the growing computing demands of artificial intelligence. We investigate high-order modulation and advanced equalization for 400 Gbps interconnects. Theoretical bit error rate (BER) expressions for 4/8-ary pulse amplitude modulation (PAM) and approximate expressions for six PAM6 formats generated from 32-ary quadrature amplitude modulation (32QAM) are derived. In additive white Gaussian noise, PAM6 generated by framed-cross 32QAM achieves the best BER performance among the PAM6 formats. PAM6 and PAM8 incur peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) penalties of approximately 4.2 and 7.2 dB, respectively, relative to PAM4 at the KP4 forward error correction (KP4-FEC) limit. Simulations compare PAM4, PAM6, and PAM8 at a line rate of 440 Gbps (net rate of 400G) under different bandwidth limitations. As bandwidth becomes more constrained, bandwidth requirements increasingly dominate performance over noise tolerance. PAM4 requires the lowest PSNR to reach the KP4-FEC limit in mildly bandwidth-limited channels, whereas PAM6 performs best under moderate limitations. PAM8 offers a significant advantage under severe limitations because of its lower bandwidth requirement and reduced susceptibility to high-frequency attenuation. With maximum likelihood sequence estimation, PAM6 and PAM8 reach the KP4-FEC limit under all evaluated channel conditions, while PAM6 requires a lower PSNR in most channels, highlighting its potential for 400G-SerDes systems.

papers.title: Connectivity-Aware Exploration of Robotic Grasp Spaces
papers.abstract: Robotic grasping is typically formulated as the problem of identifying successful actions from a space of candidate grasp poses. However, the organization of successful actions within this space has received less attention. We study the multiscale structure of viable robotic grasps in SE(3) and investigate whether this structure can be exploited for more efficient exploration. Using a large-scale grasp dataset, we show that successful grasp sets exhibit heterogeneous and reproducible connectivity structure across objects. We then introduce a connectivity-aware sampling strategy that incrementally explores the currently observed grasp space by prioritizing potential bridges between components, structural frontiers, boundary extensions, and geometric novelty. In controlled reconstruction experiments, the method recovers the connectivity structure of successful grasp sets substantially more efficiently than random sampling and farthest-point sampling. We further evaluate whether connectivity acquired under hidden grasp viability can improve subsequent grasp discovery, and whether structural experience from previously explored objects can be retrieved and transferred to unseen objects. These results suggest that the spatial organization of viable actions provides information relevant to grasp-space exploration beyond the viability of individual candidate actions. More broadly, they motivate structure-aware exploration as a means of exploiting the geometry of viable action spaces in robotic manipulation.

papers.title: CHOREO: From Single Skill to Continuous Humanoid Execution
papers.abstract: Motion data, RL policies, and generative models give humanoids thousands of skills, and the best general trackers execute nearly all of them alone. Chained to follow a language instruction, the skills fail far more often: in simulation, even the best of eight trackers reaches only 84.9\% sequence success, and their average is 48.9\%. This is because validating a skill alone certifies it only for the tracker that ran it and the state it started from, whereas a sequence keeps one tracker and starts each skill wherever the last one ended. Prior work meets these two conditions mostly by training; CHOREO restores them without retraining by treating every skill as a trajectory that any tracker can run. It assigns each instruction the most precise of its best-validated frozen trackers, which ends each skill closer to the next one's start. It then builds each transition from the measured robot state, escalating to bridges and standing only when needed. On 400 instructions, CHOREO lifts sequence success to 95.8\% and beats always standing between skills by 2.8 points with 42\% shorter transitions. On a physical Unitree G1, all 45 zero-shot trials of nine five-action instructions succeed.

papers.title: The Complexity of Computing Class Probabilities in BID Probabilistic Databases
papers.abstract: We study the problem of computing class probabilities in block-independent disjoint (BID) probabilistic databases. Given the probability with which each block in the database realizes each feasible tuple type, the goal is to compute the probability of a class of worlds specified by a given tuple multiplicity vector, thus grouping together worlds with the same bag (multiset) of realized tuple types. For this problem, we prove $\#\mathsf{P}$-hardness even for very restricted and structured inputs. On the other hand, we show that it admits an FPRAS, as well as $\mathsf{XP}$-time algorithms parameterized by the number of tuple types and the treewidth of an incidence graph modeling the connections between blocks and tuples. Finally, we show that augmenting the problem with certain compatibility constraints between block realizations renders it $\#\mathsf{XLP}$- and $\#\mathsf{XALP}$-hard parameterized by pathwidth and treewidth respectively, ruling out $\mathsf{FPT}$ algorithms under standard assumptions. We leave as an open question whether this also holds in the absence of compatibility constraints.

papers.title: Functional Renormalization for Random Matrix Theory: The relational background field method
papers.abstract: The construction of a reliable renormalization group (RG) flow for discrete gravity models that preserves their underlying symmetry group, typically $U(N)$ or $O(N)$, remains an open problem. For random matrix models, which are the focus of this paper, this symmetry is intrinsically tied to the interactions encoding the random geometry of two-dimensional quantum Euclidean spacetime. We develop a novel approach based on the introduction of a partial matrix-valued intermediate field. In the large-$N$ limit, measure concentration strongly suppresses fluctuations of its singular values, allowing it to play the role of a self-consistent background field. This provides the basis for a relational RG in which the notion of scale is dynamically induced by the effective Gaussian measure in the basis where the intermediate field is diagonal. Our construction preserves the symmetry of the original model and admits a well-defined continuum limit. We show that the resulting infrared theory is described by a three-dimensional non-local Euclidean field theory with a non-trivial Wilson-Fisher-like fixed point and a single relevant direction. Remarkably, the associated critical exponent exactly matches the standard double-scaling exponent. We finally discuss extensions of the background-field approach to other discrete gravity models, such as random tensor models, and to different symmetry groups, as well as connections with more formal RG frameworks and information geometry.

papers.title: Higher-Order Interactions in Complex Systems: Mechanisms, Behaviour, Representation and Reducibility
papers.abstract: Higher-order interactions couple three or more elements in ways not decomposable into pairwise contributions. They are associated with phenomenological signatures, collective thermodynamic or dynamical properties such as explosive synchronization and discontinuous transitions. Neither such signatures nor a many-body description establishes a many-body mechanism, since both depend on how the system is represented. Connecting work on higher-order network dynamics and multivariate statistical dependence, this review distinguishes the mechanism governing a system, the behaviour it produces and how either is represented. Behaviour comprises phenomenological signatures and statistical dependence. Representation covers which variables are included and how relations are encoded. We examine direct many-body mechanisms, nonlinear but pairwise mechanisms producing similar signatures, indirect routes through shared environments or eliminated variables, and temporal aggregation, an artefact of observation. The same behaviour can arise from different mechanisms, and a higher-order mechanism has no universal behavioural consequence. We formulate reducibility, whether a higher-order model can be replaced by a lower-order one, relative to an admissible model class, a target and a tolerance, and apply it to synchronization, ecology, statistical mechanics and contagion. Information-theoretic and inferential methods are reviewed for detecting higher-order dependence, testing lower-order alternatives and reconstructing interaction structure. What data can establish about the model is a question of identifiability, distinct from reducibility. Observational data alone cannot uniquely establish the mechanism without structural assumptions, resolved dynamics or interventions. We close with open problems in linking mechanisms to measurable signatures, coarse-graining, identifiability and causality. (Abridged)

papers.title: Proposing, never assigning: fair allocation of shifts in experimental particle physics collaborations from ranked wishes under institutional quotas
papers.abstract: Experimental particle physics collaborations staff the operation of their detectors with shifts, taken in the control room or remotely by members drawn from dozens of institutions. The established practice for filling them is a credit system with self sign-up: institutions owe a quota of credit, and people take the seats they want when booking opens. This paper describes a method in which seats are instead allocated from ranked wishes under institutional quotas, the result is issued as offers that each person accepts or declines, and an independent checker recomputes every rule before anything is published: the platform proposes, never assigns, and proves that it kept the rules. The credit and quota model is inherited from current practice. Around that core the paper adds a quota rule that keeps indivisible blocks fair to institutions whose share of a period is smaller than one block, and four rules that make fairness visible beyond the count: shares of owl, weekend and holiday blocks, seats shown in the laboratory's clock and the institution's own, reachable pools for institutions that cannot travel, and booking order by balance. On a synthetic collaboration of 48 institutions and 256 eligible members, the method allocates 70 to 72 of 72 seats per period in two rounds, with a mean rank satisfaction of 84 to 95% and no rule broken; after a year of running every institution of four members or more is within 13% of its cumulative share, and the smallest institutions, which one block overshoots by arithmetic, are brought within the same range by pooling in pairs. The method is stated completely enough to be reimplemented; a reference implementation exists and is available to collaborations under license. It applies as it stands to any scientific collaboration that staffs a facility in blocks of shifts under institutional quotas.

papers.title: Radial Limits and Euler Exponents of a False Theta Series with Character Modulo 8
papers.abstract: Let $T_k=k(k+1)/2$ and let $N_n(q)$ be the series with terms $(-1)^{T_k}(2k+1)^{2n+1}q^{T_k}$ for $k\ge 0$. We study the false theta function $D=N_0$ and the moment quotients $N_n/D$. We prove an exact transformation formula for twists of even order. It expresses each moment as a convergent series of derivatives of the Dawson integral, with the dual twist and its phase determined by a quadratic Gauss sum. The formula gives the finite radial values of the moments at roots of unity as nonzero cyclotomic integers and yields congruences between them. Inside the unit disc we consider the quotient of $D$ by the theta series with terms $(-1)^{T_k}q^{T_k}$. Each nonconstant coefficient of this quotient is minus twice a positive integer that counts divisors and restricted partitions. These counts give a Lyndon-word formula for the exponents in the formal Euler product of $D$. The factorization also identifies the unique real zero in $(-1,1)$. A comparison with a cubic polynomial shows that this simple zero is the only zero in $|q|<1/2$.

papers.title: A Single-Loop Method with Optimal Leading-Order Oracle Complexity for Optimization and Game Stationarity in Nonconvex--Concave Minimax Optimization
papers.abstract: We develop a single-loop first-order framework for smooth nonconvex--concave minimax optimization, with matching leading-order upper and lower bounds for optimization and game stationarity in a projected zero-respecting oracle model. We propose a single-loop projected damped extragradient method coupling projected extragradient updates with dual momentum and a moving proximal center. Each iteration uses at most three gradient evaluations, without nested subproblems. For game stationarity, a deterministic best iterate has first-order residual below $\varepsilon$ with leading oracle complexity $\mathcal{O}(L^{3/2}D_Y^{1/2}Δ_ϕ\varepsilon^{-5/2})$, where $L$ is the gradient Lipschitz constant, $D_Y$ bounds the dual feasible-set diameter, and $Δ_ϕ$ is the initial-point-dependent value-function gap. For optimization stationarity, a uniformly selected iterate has expected squared Moreau-envelope gradient norm at most $\varepsilon^2$ with leading oracle complexity $\mathcal{O}(L^2D_YΔ_ϕ\varepsilon^{-3})$. Matching lower bounds are $Ω(L^{3/2}D_Y^{1/2}Δ_ϕ\varepsilon^{-5/2})$ for game stationarity and $Ω(L^2D_YΔ_ϕ\varepsilon^{-3})$ for optimization stationarity over projected zero-respecting first-order methods. Under dual strong concavity, the same framework achieves leading first-order oracle complexity $\mathcal{O}(\sqrtκLΔ_ϕ\varepsilon^{-2})$ under both criteria, where $κ$ is the dual condition number. Matching lower bounds hold for both criteria in the same oracle model. To our knowledge, this is the first work to close the oracle complexity gap for smooth nonconvex--concave minimax optimization under both stationarity criteria by simultaneously improving upper and lower bounds in the projected zero-respecting oracle model.

papers.title: Self-Distilled Pronunciation and Accent Control for Neural Text-to-Speech
papers.abstract: Text-to-speech that reads raw text has no lexicon: a rare word is read as guessed, and a native Japanese listener accepts a word only if its reading and pitch accent are both right. A known remedy installs a reading-and-accent channel into a released model, but it needs many recordings. This paper removes the recordings: the frozen backbone reads a sentence containing a common word it already says correctly, and that output serves as the teacher for the same sentence with the word replaced by an annotated reading with its pitch accent. Screened raters judged the tag right on 0.80 to 0.93 of unseen difficult words on four backbones spanning autoregressive, diffusion, and encoder-decoder synthesis; plain kana, which cannot express an accent, got 0.38 to 0.60. On words needing no edit, naturalness is non-inferior on one backbone; on the other three, listeners prefer the unedited rendition by 0.19 to 0.26.

papers.title: Stripe-Like Superconducting Enhancement and Coexisting Magnetic Texture in an Infinite Layer Nickelate
papers.abstract: Despite their promise as structural and electronic analogs to cuprates, nickelate thin films consistently exhibit broadened superconducting transitions in many experiments that remain poorly understood. Local measurements are ideal for revealing the presence of defects or competing phases, which may cause this transition broadening through a phase-separation. Here, we use scanning SQUID microscopy to investigate local superfluid density and magnetic texture of optimally doped $\mathrm{Nd}_{1-x}\mathrm{Eu}_{x}\mathrm{NiO}_{2}$ (NENO) (x=0.25) grown via molecular beam epitaxy. We observed a weakly-magnetic texture coexisting with superconductivity. Spatially resolved susceptibility imaging reveals a highly non-uniform superconducting state, characterized by a robust stripe-like enhancement pattern appearing near the phase transition. By resolving the mesoscopic landscape of electronic and magnetic inhomogeneities, these findings suggest that a competing magnetic phase is a primary contributor to the unusually broad superconducting transitions of these optimally doped NENO samples. Understanding the uncovered superconducting enhancement may provide a path to raising superconducting temperatures in these materials.

papers.title: Physics as the label for measuring and correcting materials reasoning in multimodal models
papers.abstract: Vision-language and language models increasingly interpret materials data, yet most benchmarks score final answers rather than whether the quantities a model states while reasoning obey established physical constraints. We introduce MatPCR, a label-free benchmark that uses six programmatic oracle families spanning diffraction geometry, microscopy scale, Raman peak structure, and Materials Project-grounded checks of near-hull stability, computed band-gap class, and net magnetization to test the physical admissibility of each checkable quantity a reasoning chain states, summarized as the Physical-Consistency Rate (PCR). The oracles are necessary-condition checks; their precision is audited by human review with interval estimates, and their recall on real responses is not assumed. Across nine models and 4,334 checkable records, overall PCR ranges from 0.556 to 0.778, and paired item-level tests separate only differences larger than about 0.07. Constraint-Grounded Self-Verification reduces oracle-detected violations in all four tested models; paired before-after scoring shows that it also raises answer correctness, but that most revisions which clear the oracle move to an admissible rather than an exact value. An open verifier reaches ROC AUC = 0.850 in distribution, varies strongly across constraint families, and does not transfer at a useful level to any held-out constraint family. An exact identity quantifies how oracle error displaces the reported PCR.

papers.title: Effects of Interaction Range on Fluid Multicriticality: A Computational Study of an Interconverting Lattice Model
papers.abstract: The range of intermolecular interactions plays a central role in determining the nature of phase behavior and critical phenomena. It is well established through studies of the Ising model that as interaction range increases, Monte Carlo simulations progressively approach meanfield predictions as the effects of critical fluctuations are suppressed. In this work, we investigate how varying interaction range influences fluid multicriticality using an interconverting lattice model that exhibits both Ising-like liquid-gas criticality and symmetric fluid tricriticality (similar to that in the superfluid $^4$He-$^3$He mixture). This minimal model serves as a representative system for exploring the evolution of competing critical points within a generic framework. We analyze the model using both meanfield theory and three-dimensional Monte Carlo simulations while systematically varying the number of interacting neighbors, $Z_n$, from 6 to 388 on a simple cubic lattice. We find that the system with nearest-neighbor interactions ($Z_n=6$) reveals only two types of multicritical behavior, while for larger interaction ranges, four distinct archetypes emerge. We demonstrate the convergence of the simulation results to those of the meanfield theory as the number of interacting neighbors tends to infinity, and we discuss the results within the framework of crossover critical phenomena.

papers.title: The phase coordinates transformation in Moyal noncommutative framework 2-dimensional harmonic oscillator and Painlevé second equation
papers.abstract: This work aims to explore the physical application of Moyal noncom- mutative formalism with the the presentation of new transformations which connect the old canonical coordinates to purly noncommuting phase coordi- nates through the parameters describe the Moyal noncommutative deforma- tion. These transformations are consistent with the Moyal noncommunica- tive brackets and build sixteen components traceless anti-symmetric tensor. This formalism incorporates space-space and space-momentum noncommu- taivity rather then noncommutativity (Heisenberg quantum commutation ) only for the canonical coordinates. The transformations imply to construct noncommutative analogs of 2-dimensional harmonic oscillator with its superintegrability and Painlevé second equation. The associated deformed Hamiltonians additionally involve some extra symmetries and reveal a deep physical understanding of about the additional symmetries with noncommunicative structure. The Painlevé second noncommutative coordinates transformation are also efficiently applied to generate the first Yablonskii Vorobev polynomial with Painlevé second parameter transformation.

papers.title: Testing PPN by the Rotation of S301 Star
